subject: jukebox
pitch: A 1950s diner jukebox. A tall rounded arch of glowing coloured tubes in red, amber and teal, chrome trim everywhere, a domed glass window showing a stack of records and the arm that picks them, rows of chrome selection buttons with little title cards, a speaker grille with a starburst pattern, and a coin slot.

I'm planning out a 1950s diner jukebox model using the agentic-3js-builder SDK, thinking through which construction functions I'll need like joints, chains, sweeps, lathes, and surface decals to build it.

Since a jukebox isn't a creature, I don't need a full rig, but I can use a joint for the moving record-picking arm and keep other parts as static props. I'm sketching the Wurlitzer-inspired design: roughly 1.5m tall with a cream/chrome plinth base, an arched cabinet body with colored tube details, a glass window revealing the mechanism, a selection button panel, and a speaker grille, all scaled realistically in meters.

I'm deciding to skip the extrude API given uncertainty about its thickness parameters, and instead build pieces directly from plain three.js geometries (boxes, cylinders, toruses, spheres) passed into b.part with position and orientation options.

For cylinders that need to run along Z instead of the default Y axis, I'll just bake a rotation into the geometry itself before passing it in, which sidesteps any ambiguity around the `dir`/`aim` semantics. I'm also thinking through the joint structure — a root joint for the cabinet with child joints for moving parts like the record-picking arm, since props can be plain objects but a mechanism like the arm probably benefits from being a small joint chain I can rotate.

Rather than relying on `b.chain` with uncertain joint-naming behavior, I think it's safer to just call `b.sweep` directly with a raw array of points as the path, skipping chain creation entirely since sweep accepts any point-array path on its own.

For the glowing neon tubes, I'm weighing whether MeshStandardMaterial even supports emissive properties through the color-string API, or whether I'd need to traverse the built object tree afterward and manually set `.material.emissive` on matching meshes — though that's risky since materials are shared per color and could affect other parts unexpectedly.

Since I can't easily track mesh identity after building, I'll settle for a simpler approach: traverse the root, find meshes using MeshStandardMaterial, and compare their colour's hex string against my known glow colours (red, amber, teal), setting emissive on matches even if it occasionally catches unrelated parts sharing the same colour.

For the chrome look, I'm considering tweaking roughness and metalness directly on those materials to fake a metallic shine, though without an environment map pure metalness could just read as dark rather than shiny.

I'm also realizing I don't actually have documented signatures for the paint, spots, stripes, countershade, or svg helpers, so using them confidently is risky without more context.

Given that, the safer path is sticking to core builder functions I do know—joint, chain, sweep, part, surface, ring, decal, cards—and constructing details like title cards and starburst patterns using plain geometry and colors rather than unverified texture helpers. For the starburst specifically, I'm thinking radial thin boxes or rays arranged around the speaker grille would be a safe geometric substitute.

I'll keep geometries centered at origin and rely on `at` for placement to avoid double-translating, assuming identity orientation by default. For the structure, I'm planning a root joint for the cabinet body and a child joint for the arm/pick mechanism, positioning it near the record window with its own `at` and `aim` values.

Since the parent/child joint syntax isn't clearly specified, the safest approach is to use a single root joint named "cabinet" and let all parts attach to it automatically, since props don't require a full skeleton like creatures do.

I'll skip extra joints and just compute all positions analytically in model space using a single root joint, placing parts with explicit coordinates.
